title: Sherpa Culture and the Monasteries of the Khumbu
meta_description: Who the Sherpas are, where they came from, their names, festivals, food and the monasteries of Tengboche, Pangboche, Thame and Khumjung, with etiquette tips.
summary: The Sherpas came from Kham in eastern Tibet about five centuries ago and settled the Khumbu and Solu valleys below Everest. They are Nyingma Buddhists, farmers, traders and, for a century, the backbone of Himalayan climbing. Here is a short guide to their history, names, monasteries, festivals and food, and how to be a good guest.

sections.heading: People from the east
paras: Sherpa means people from the east in their own language, from shar, east, and pa, people. Their ancestors lived in Kham, in eastern Tibet, and migrated west and then south across the Himalaya about five hundred years ago, according to Sherpa clan histories. The route they remember is the Nangpa La, a glacier pass at the head of the Bhote Koshi valley above Thame. They settled first in the Khumbu, the high valleys below Everest, and in Solu, the greener hills to the south, which Sherpas call Shorong.

For centuries the Khumbu Sherpas lived by herding yaks, growing barley, buckwheat and, from the nineteenth century, potatoes, which changed the high valleys by letting families farm at altitude. They also traded across the Nangpa La, carrying grain and goods north and bringing salt, wool and Tibetan items south. Namche Bazaar grew as a trading village on that route long before it became a trekking town.

From the 1920s Sherpas from Solukhumbu who had moved to Darjeeling found work as porters on British expeditions to Everest from the Tibetan side. Their skill and strength made them famous, and Tenzing Norgay, who grew up in Thame, reached the summit with Edmund Hillary on 29 May 1953. Today Sherpa is both an ethnic name and, loosely, a job title for high-altitude workers, though many high-altitude workers are not ethnic Sherpas, and many Sherpas have nothing to do with climbing.

sections.heading: Names that tell the day you were born
paras: Many Sherpa first names come from the day of the week on which a person was born, a custom shared with Tibetans. So if you meet three men called Pasang on the trail, they were all born on a Friday. A second name, often given by a lama, follows. Sherpa as a surname is a modern addition used on documents; within the community, a person's clan, ru in Sherpa, and home village carry more meaning, and people from the same clan traditionally do not marry. Learning a guide's name and asking which day it stands for is a good way to start a conversation.

sections.heading: The monasteries you will pass
paras: Sherpas follow the Nyingma school, the oldest of the four main schools of Tibetan Buddhism, which traces itself to Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, who brought Buddhism to Tibet in the eighth century. Every village has a gompa, a temple, and the larger ones have communities of monks or nuns.

Tengboche, on a saddle at 3,867 m facing Everest and Ama Dablam, is the best known. It was founded in 1916 by Lama Gulu, with links to Rongbuk Monastery on the Tibetan side of Everest. An earthquake destroyed it in 1934, and a fire in 1989 burned it again; each time it was rebuilt, the second time with help from donors in Nepal and abroad. It holds the Mani Rimdu festival each autumn and an afternoon puja most days.

Pangboche gompa, above the village at about 3,985 m, is said to be the oldest in the Khumbu. Local tradition credits Lama Sangwa Dorje, a revered figure in Sherpa history, with founding it in the seventeenth century. Thame gompa, built against a cliff above Thame, also dates back several centuries and holds its own Mani Rimdu in spring. Khumjung gompa is famous for a relic villagers call the yeti scalp, kept in a glass case; scientific tests in 1960 suggested it was made from the skin of a serow, a Himalayan goat-antelope.
In Solu, Chiwong monastery near Phaplu, founded in 1923, and the large community of Thupten Chholing near Junbesi, founded by Trulshik Rinpoche after he left Tibet in 1959, are worth the walk.

sections.heading: Sacred mountains and protector gods
paras: For Sherpas the mountains are not empty rock. Khumbila, the dark peak of about 5,761 m above Khumjung and Namche, is the home of Khumbu Yul Lha, the protector deity of the region, often painted riding a white horse. Out of respect it has never been climbed. Everest, Chomolungma, is linked to Miyolangsangma, a goddess of generosity, one of the five sisters of long life. Before every expedition, Sherpa climbers hold a puja at base camp to ask her permission and protection, building a stone altar, burning juniper and hanging prayer flags.

You will also see the practice of everyday faith: mani walls carved with om mani padme hum, prayer wheels turned by hand, water and wind, chortens holding relics, and prayer flags printed with the wind horse, lungta, which carries prayers on the wind. Juniper, shukpa, is burned in the morning as an offering. Walk to the left of mani walls and chortens so that they stay on your right, the way a Sherpa walks.

sections.heading: Festivals of the year
paras: The biggest celebration is Losar, the Tibetan new year, in February or March, when families clean their houses, cook special foods and visit monasteries. In summer, Dumji is held in the main Khumbu villages, with masked dances, feasts and the whole village gathering in the gompa courtyard; sponsorship rotates among families. Mani Rimdu, the best-known festival for visitors, is held at Tengboche in October or November, at Thame in spring and at Chiwong in Solu in autumn. Dates follow the lunar calendar and change every year.
Visitors are welcome at most festival days. Dress warmly, sit where your guide suggests, keep your voice low during rituals and do not use flash photography.

sections.heading: What Sherpas eat and drink
paras: Lodge menus are full of pancakes and pizza, but ask for Sherpa food and the kitchen will often cook it. Shyakpa is a thick stew of hand-torn noodles, potato, radish and sometimes yak meat, ideal on a cold evening. Riki kur are potato pancakes, grated and fried on a griddle, eaten with yak butter or a sour cheese called somar. Tsampa, roasted barley flour, is mixed with butter tea into a dough. Butter tea, solja, is salty, rich and very warming; Sherpa hosts refill your cup again and again. Chhang, a home-brewed barley or millet beer, is offered at festivals and weddings.

Meals in a Sherpa kitchen centre on the hearth, where the senior woman of the house usually cooks and serves. Guests sit on benches along the wall; the place nearest the hearth and altar is for honoured guests and elders, so wait to be shown where to sit.

sections.heading: Being a good guest
paras: Sherpa families are used to visitors, generous and good-humoured. A few habits make a real difference to how you are received.
list: Greet people with tashi delek; say thuche che for thank you.
Walk clockwise around chortens and gompas, and keep mani walls on your right.
Remove shoes and hat before entering a prayer hall, and do not point your feet at the altar or at people.
Ask before photographing monks, rituals or people; inside prayer halls, photography is usually not allowed.
Leave a small donation in the box at monasteries you visit; NPR 100–500 is usual.
Accept tea or food with both hands or with your right hand, not your left.
Do not touch religious objects or sit on mani stones and prayer walls.
Dress modestly in villages and monasteries, with shoulders and knees covered.

faqs.q: Where did the Sherpa people come from?
faqs.a: The Sherpas came from Kham in eastern Tibet. According to their own clan histories they migrated across the Himalaya about five hundred years ago, crossing the Nangpa La above Thame into the Khumbu, and then spread into Solu. Their name means people from the east. They speak Sherpa, a Tibetic language, and follow Nyingma Buddhism.

faqs.q: Is Sherpa a job or an ethnic group?
faqs.a: Both, loosely. Sherpa is an ethnic group from Solukhumbu, but on expeditions the word is often used for any high-altitude worker, many of whom are Tamang, Rai or Gurung. Many Sherpas work in tourism, but others are farmers, teachers, doctors and business owners in Kathmandu and abroad.

faqs.q: What is the oldest monastery in the Khumbu?
faqs.a: Pangboche gompa is usually described as the oldest, traditionally said to have been founded in the seventeenth century by Lama Sangwa Dorje, a revered figure in Sherpa history. Thame gompa is also several centuries old. Tengboche, the best known, is younger: it was founded in 1916 and rebuilt after an earthquake in 1934 and a fire in 1989.

Yes. Visitors can enter the courtyard and usually the prayer hall when it is open, and sit quietly at the back of the afternoon puja, typically around 3 pm. Remove your shoes and hat, do not take photographs inside, and leave a small donation. During Mani Rimdu in October or November, the public festival days are open to everyone.

faqs.q: Why do Sherpas have the same names?
faqs.a: Many Sherpa first names come from the day of the week a person was born, so many people share names such as Pasang, Friday, or Lhakpa, Wednesday. A second name is often given by a lama. Among themselves, Sherpas are also known by clan, village and family, which helps tell people apart.

faqs.q: What is the yeti scalp at Khumjung?
faqs.a: Khumjung monastery keeps a conical, hair-covered relic that villagers call the yeti scalp. It was examined in 1960 during an expedition led by Edmund Hillary, and tests suggested it had been made from the skin of a serow, a Himalayan goat-antelope. It remains a respected object at the monastery and can be seen for a small donation.

faqs.q: Why has Khumbila never been climbed?
faqs.a: Khumbila, about 5,761 m, rises above Khumjung and Namche and is believed to be the home of Khumbu Yul Lha, the protector deity of the Khumbu. Out of respect for him, Sherpas regard the summit as sacred and do not climb it. You will see his image, a figure on a white horse, painted in local monasteries.

faqs.q: What Sherpa food should I try?
faqs.a: Try shyakpa, a hearty stew of hand-torn noodles, potatoes and vegetables, sometimes with yak meat; riki kur, grated potato pancakes with butter or somar cheese; tsampa, roasted barley flour; and solja, salty butter tea. Lodges in Namche, Khumjung and Thame will often cook them on request, especially in the evening.

Tashi delek is the everyday greeting in Sherpa and Tibetan, used like hello and good wishes together; it carries the sense of blessings and good fortune. Say it with a smile and a slight nod when you meet people on the trail. Thuche che means thank you.
